title: Leading Change in Schools
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes reflects on a year of leading professional development at scale across a trust, asking why school change still fails despite widespread training in the EEF implementation model. Drawing on Kotter's stages of change, she argues that change fails when it is treated as a launch rather than a learning process, and that leaders must centre the why and then build conditions for staff agency. She walks through the stages: naming a concrete pupil-learning problem, building a coalition with classroom credibility, making new practice learnable through modelling and rehearsal, and removing barriers rather than piling expectations onto unchanged systems. Throughout she candidly names her own mistakes, including designing principles alone and failing to change the systems that would have supported the CPD. A key distinction is between non-negotiable purpose and negotiable implementation, and between consistency and uniformity. She concludes that leading change is about helping professionals learn better ways of solving real problems for pupils.
points: Hughes argues that CPD too often begins with the solution ('we are introducing whole-class feedback') instead of a concrete pupil problem, producing thin compliance that does not survive pressure.
She insists the guiding coalition needs classroom credibility, including middle leaders, early career teachers and sceptical voices, so middle leaders become co-authors rather than delivery agents.
Her practical tool for agency is separating non-negotiable purpose (e.g. checking for understanding before independent practice) from negotiable implementation such as subject-specific routines.
She names her biggest mistake as adding expectations without removing anything, arguing that even world-leading CPD fails when marking policies, meeting time and assessment systems stay unchanged.
She distinguishes consistency (shared intent and reliable quality) from uniformity (everyone doing the same visible thing), arguing the first supports professionalism and the second drains it.
quotes: In schools, this happens when leaders announce a new initiative and assume that agreement in the hall will become action in the classroom. It rarely does.
But if the why is unclear, staff will experience the change as another demand. They may comply, but compliance is thin. It does not survive pressure.
But middle leaders have not shaped it, tested it or built ownership. They become delivery agents rather than co-authors. That is a mistake.
Agency starts before implementation. Staff are more motivated when they have some influence over the shape of the work. This does not mean every decision is put to a vote.
This is the biggest mistake I have made this year. If the systems aren’t there, even the most world leading CPD will fail.
